course.title: N4 actions, views, and methods
course.description: A source-grounded bridge into decisions, preparation, attempts, judgments, limits, and ways of doing things.

chapters.title: Actions and intentions
chapters.description: Make plans, prepare, try, and describe help in everyday Japanese.

lessons.title: Actions and intentions
lessons.subtitle: 行動と予定
lessons.description: Use ten N4 patterns to talk about choices, preparation, attempts, and favors.

chapters.title: Views and methods
chapters.description: Describe direction, certainty, appearance, limits, degree, and ways of doing things.

lessons.title: Views and methods
lessons.subtitle: 見方と方法
lessons.description: Use ten more N4 patterns to follow change, judge situations, and explain how to act.

chapters.title: Conditions and results
chapters.description: Compare conditions, expected results, and advice in practical situations.

lessons.title: Conditions and results
lessons.subtitle: 条件と結果
lessons.description: Use と、たら、ば、 and なら to connect conditions to natural results and advice.

chapters.title: Ability and possibility
chapters.description: Say what you can do and compare compact potential forms with explicit ability expressions.

lessons.title: Ability and possibility
lessons.subtitle: 可能と能力
lessons.description: Use potential verbs and ことができる to describe practical ability without confusing potential and passive meanings.

chapters.title: Passive situations
chapters.description: Describe who was affected by an action and distinguish passive meaning from ability.

lessons.title: Passive situations
lessons.subtitle: 受身の場面
lessons.description: Use basic passive forms with people and objects, while checking context against potential readings.

chapters.title: Causing and allowing
chapters.description: Describe who makes or lets another person do an action in basic everyday situations.

lessons.title: Causing and allowing
lessons.subtitle: 使役の場面
lessons.description: Use basic godan and ichidan causative forms with clear causee roles and practical contexts.

chapters.title: Plans and proposals
chapters.description: Use volitional forms for decisions, proposals, and intentions about what to do next.

lessons.title: Plans and proposals
lessons.subtitle: 意向と計画
lessons.description: Form よう and おう, then connect the form to a clear plan or intention with と思います.

chapters.title: Giving and receiving
chapters.description: Track the direction of a gift or favor from the giver's and receiver's perspective.

lessons.title: Giving and receiving
lessons.subtitle: 授受の視点
lessons.description: Use あげる, くれる, and もらう as one perspective system before extending it with て-form helpers.

chapters.title: Resulting states and past continuity
chapters.description: Use てある and ていた to describe prepared states and actions or states that held in the past.

lessons.title: Resulting states and past continuity
lessons.subtitle: 状態と過去
lessons.description: Extend the existing て-form family with intentional result states and past ongoing context.

grammar.title: ことにする
grammar.formation: Verb plain form + ことにする.
grammar.intuition: ことにする turns a decision into a chosen plan the speaker will carry out.
usageConditions: Use it for a decision or resolution made by the subject.
Use the negative form when deciding not to do something.

examples.japanese: 毎日、日本語を勉強することにしました。
examples.translation: I decided to study Japanese every day.

examples.japanese: 今日は電車で帰ることにします。
examples.translation: I will decide to go home by train today.

examples.japanese: 毎朝、早く起きることにしました。
examples.translation: I decided to get up early every morning.

examples.japanese: 会議には参加しないことにします。
examples.translation: I will decide not to attend the meeting.

commonMistakes: Do not use ことにする for a plan that is only an intention; compare つもり.
Keep the verb before ことにする in plain form.

grammar.title: ずに
grammar.formation: Verb negative stem + ずに; する becomes せずに.
grammar.intuition: ずに removes an action from the sequence while the main action still happens.
usageConditions: Use it when the subject does one action without doing another.
する is irregular: 勉強する becomes 勉強せずに.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べずに、家を出ました。
examples.translation: I left home without eating breakfast.

examples.japanese: 何も言わずに、部屋を出てください。
examples.translation: Please leave the room without saying anything.

examples.japanese: コーヒーを飲まずに仕事を始めました。
examples.translation: I started work without drinking coffee.

examples.japanese: 辞書を使わずに読んでみます。
examples.translation: I will try reading without using a dictionary.

commonMistakes: Do not attach ずに directly to the dictionary form.
Remember the irregular する → せずに change.

grammar.title: そうだ（様態）
grammar.formation: Verb stem or い-adjective stem + そうだ; remove い from い-adjectives.
grammar.intuition: そうだ lets the speaker judge an appearance from what they can see.
usageConditions: Use the appearance meaning, not the hearsay そうだ pattern.
いい changes to よさそう before そうだ.

examples.japanese: このケーキはおいしそうです。
examples.translation: This cake looks delicious.

examples.japanese: 雨が降りそうなので、傘を持って行きます。
examples.translation: It looks like it will rain, so I will take an umbrella.

examples.japanese: 彼は眠そうです。
examples.translation: He looks sleepy.

examples.japanese: この荷物は重そうですね。
examples.translation: This luggage looks heavy.

commonMistakes: Do not keep the final い in an い-adjective before appearance そうだ.
Do not confuse appearance そうだ with reported information.

grammar.title: つもり
grammar.formation: Verb plain form + つもり; negative plans use つもりはない.
grammar.intuition: つもり presents an intention the speaker currently holds.
usageConditions: Use it for a personal plan or intention.
Use はない to say that something is not planned.

examples.japanese: 来年、日本へ行くつもりです。
examples.translation: I intend to go to Japan next year.

examples.japanese: 週末は何もしないつもりです。
examples.translation: I do not plan to do anything this weekend.

examples.japanese: 夏休みに京都へ行くつもりです。
examples.translation: I intend to go to Kyoto during summer vacation.

examples.japanese: 今日は出かけないつもりです。
examples.translation: I do not plan to go out today.

commonMistakes: つもり describes an intention, not a completed action.
Keep the verb before つもり in plain form.

grammar.title: てあげる
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + あげる.
grammar.intuition: てあげる frames an action as a favor offered to another person.
usageConditions: Name the recipient with に when needed.
Use it carefully when the favor could sound self-congratulatory.

examples.japanese: 友達に本を貸してあげました。
examples.translation: I lent a book to my friend.

examples.japanese: 母に花を買ってあげます。
examples.translation: I will buy flowers for my mother.

examples.japanese: 妹に宿題を教えてあげました。
examples.translation: I helped my younger sister with her homework.

examples.japanese: 駅まで送ってあげましょうか。
examples.translation: Shall I take you to the station?

commonMistakes: Do not use the wrong verb form before あげる.
Consider the relationship before presenting an action as a favor.

grammar.title: ておく
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + おく.
grammar.intuition: ておく marks preparation done before a later need.
usageConditions: Use it when the result is intentionally left ready.
In casual speech, ておく may contract to とく.

examples.japanese: 旅行の前に、ホテルを予約しておきます。
examples.translation: I will reserve the hotel before the trip.

examples.japanese: 必要な資料を机の上に置いておきました。
examples.translation: I left the necessary documents on the desk.

examples.japanese: 出発する前に、切符を買っておきます。
examples.translation: I will buy the tickets in advance before departing.

examples.japanese: 名前を紙に書いておいてください。
examples.translation: Please write your name on the paper beforehand.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse preparation ておく with simple sequence て.
The earlier action is done with a later situation in mind.

grammar.title: てくれる
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + くれる.
grammar.intuition: てくれる presents another person's action as a benefit received by the speaker or their group.
usageConditions: Use it when the action benefits the speaker or someone close to them.
The helper is normally marked by が or は.

examples.japanese: 先生が漢字を教えてくれました。
examples.translation: The teacher taught me kanji.

examples.japanese: 友達が駅まで案内してくれます。
examples.translation: My friend will guide me to the station.

examples.japanese: 友達が荷物を持ってくれました。
examples.translation: My friend carried my luggage for me.

examples.japanese: 母が駅まで迎えに来てくれます。
examples.translation: My mother will come to pick me up at the station.

commonMistakes: Do not swap the beneficiary perspective with てあげる.
Keep the benefitting person clear from the context.

grammar.title: てしまう
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + しまう.
grammar.intuition: てしまう highlights completion or an unwanted result the speaker regrets.
usageConditions: Use it for a completed action when completion matters.
It can also signal regret or an accidental outcome.

examples.japanese: 宿題を全部してしまいました。
examples.translation: I finished all the homework.

examples.japanese: 電車に傘を忘れてしまいました。
examples.translation: Unfortunately, I left my umbrella on the train.

examples.japanese: 電車の中で寝てしまいました。
examples.translation: I accidentally fell asleep on the train.

examples.japanese: この本を今日中に読んでしまいます。
examples.translation: I will finish reading this book today.

commonMistakes: Do not assume every てしまう sentence is negative.
Separate completion from regret using context.

grammar.title: てみる
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + みる.
grammar.intuition: てみる frames an action as an attempt or experiment.
usageConditions: Use it when trying something new or checking what happens.
The main verb stays in て-form before みる.

examples.japanese: 新しい料理を作ってみます。
examples.translation: I will try making a new dish.

examples.japanese: 分からない言葉を辞書で調べてみました。
examples.translation: I tried looking up the unknown word in a dictionary.

examples.japanese: 分からない漢字を聞いてみました。
examples.translation: I tried asking about the kanji I did not understand.

examples.japanese: 週末に新しい店へ行ってみます。
examples.translation: I will try going to a new shop this weekend.

commonMistakes: てみる is not the same as simply doing an action.
Do not use the dictionary form directly before みる.

grammar.title: てもらう
grammar.meaning: receive the favor of someone doing
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + もらう.
grammar.intuition: てもらう focuses on the speaker receiving help from another person.
usageConditions: Mark the helper with に when needed.
Use it to describe requested or appreciated assistance.

examples.japanese: 先生に作文を見てもらいました。
examples.translation: I had the teacher look over my composition.

examples.japanese: 友達に駅を教えてもらいます。
examples.translation: I will have my friend tell me the station.

examples.japanese: 友達に写真を撮ってもらいました。
examples.translation: I had my friend take a photo.

examples.japanese: 先生にもう一度説明してもらいます。
examples.translation: I will have the teacher explain it once more.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse the receiver perspective with てくれる.
The person receiving the help is the grammatical focus.

grammar.title: ていく
grammar.meaning: go and do; continue from now on
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + いく.
grammar.intuition: ていく points an action or change away from the current point and into the future.
usageConditions: Use it for an action done while going away or for a change that continues forward.
The continuing meaning is understood from the surrounding time and direction.

examples.japanese: 明日、荷物を持っていきます。
examples.translation: I will take the luggage with me tomorrow.

examples.japanese: これからも日本語を勉強していきます。
examples.translation: I will keep studying Japanese from now on.

examples.japanese: 町の景色は少しずつ変わっていきます。
examples.translation: The town scenery will gradually change.

examples.japanese: この道をまっすぐ歩いていってください。
examples.translation: Please keep walking straight along this road.

commonMistakes: Confusing the future direction of ていく with the return or approach of てくる.
Dropping the て-form before いく.

grammar.title: てくる
grammar.meaning: come and do; return after doing; begin to
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + くる.
grammar.intuition: てくる brings an action or change toward the current point or speaker.
usageConditions: Use it for doing something and coming back or for a change that has begun to appear.
Context distinguishes physical return from change over time.

examples.japanese: ちょっと飲み物を買ってきます。
examples.translation: I will go buy a drink and come back.

examples.japanese: だんだん寒くなってきました。
examples.translation: It has gradually started to get cold.

examples.japanese: 最近、日本語が少し分かってきました。
examples.translation: Recently, I have started to understand a little Japanese.

examples.japanese: 駅で友達を待ってきます。
examples.translation: I will go wait for my friend at the station and come back.

commonMistakes: Confusing an emerging change with the forward continuation of ていく.
Dropping the て-form before くる.

grammar.title: に違いない
grammar.formation: Plain form + に違いない.
grammar.intuition: に違いない presents a strong conclusion based on the speaker's evidence or judgment.
usageConditions: Use it when the speaker is highly confident in an inference.
Attach it to the plain form, including a noun or な-adjective without だ in formal writing when appropriate.

examples.japanese: 彼はもう駅に着いたに違いありません。
examples.translation: He must have arrived at the station already.

examples.japanese: この料理は人気があるに違いない。
examples.translation: This dish must be popular.

examples.japanese: あの店はもう閉まったに違いありません。
examples.translation: That shop must already be closed.

examples.japanese: 彼はこの町をよく知っているに違いない。
examples.translation: He must know this town well.

commonMistakes: Using polite ます-form directly before に違いない.
Using it when the speaker has no basis for strong confidence.

grammar.title: に決まっている
grammar.formation: Plain form + に決まっている.
grammar.intuition: に決まっている states the speaker's emphatic conviction that something is certain.
usageConditions: Use it for a firm, often conversational judgment.
The strength can sound emphatic, so match it to the situation and relationship.

examples.japanese: あの人は合格するに決まっています。
examples.translation: That person is certain to pass.

examples.japanese: この店の料理はおいしいに決まっている。
examples.translation: The food at this restaurant is definitely delicious.

examples.japanese: そんな話は本当ではないに決まっています。
examples.translation: That story is definitely not true.

examples.japanese: 明日は忙しいに決まっている。
examples.translation: Tomorrow will certainly be busy.

commonMistakes: Treating に決まっている as a neutral probability statement.
Attaching it to an inflected polite ending instead of the proposition.

grammar.title: みたい
grammar.formation: Noun + みたい; plain clause + みたい.
grammar.intuition: みたい makes a comparison or a casual judgment about how something appears.
usageConditions: Use it in conversational language for resemblance or an appearance-based impression.
When it modifies a noun, use みたいな before the noun.

examples.japanese: この雲は犬みたいです。
examples.translation: This cloud looks like a dog.

examples.japanese: 明日は雨みたいです。
examples.translation: It seems like it will rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: あの建物は学校みたいです。
examples.translation: That building looks like a school.

examples.japanese: 彼は先生みたいな話し方をします。
examples.translation: He speaks in a way that is like a teacher.

commonMistakes: Forgetting な before a following noun.
Treating a casual appearance judgment as confirmed information.

grammar.title: らしい
grammar.meaning: seems like; I heard; typical of
grammar.formation: Plain form or noun + らしい.
grammar.intuition: らしい can mark reported or inferred information, and can also describe something characteristic of a type.
usageConditions: Use context to distinguish hearsay or inference from the meaning of typicality.
Keep the clause before らしい in the plain form.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは来週引っ越すらしいです。
examples.translation: I hear that Tanaka is moving next week.

examples.japanese: 今日は春らしい暖かい日です。
examples.translation: Today is a warm day typical of spring.

examples.japanese: 来週は雪が降るらしいです。
examples.translation: I hear it will snow next week.

examples.japanese: 今日は秋らしい涼しい朝です。
examples.translation: Today is a cool morning typical of autumn.

commonMistakes: Using らしい as if it always meant direct visual appearance.
Forgetting that a noun can also be followed directly by らしい.

grammar.title: わけにはいかない
grammar.formation: Verb dictionary form + わけにはいかない; negative form + わけにはいかない expresses cannot fail to.
grammar.intuition: わけにはいかない says that circumstances, responsibility, or social expectations make an action impossible to accept.
usageConditions: Use it for a practical or social constraint, not merely physical inability.
The exact meaning depends on whether the verb is positive or negative.

examples.japanese: 明日は試験なので、遊んでいるわけにはいきません。
examples.translation: I cannot afford to spend time playing because I have an exam tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 大切な約束を忘れるわけにはいかない。
examples.translation: I cannot allow myself to forget an important promise.

examples.japanese: 約束したので、行かないわけにはいきません。
examples.translation: Because I made a promise, I cannot fail to go.

examples.japanese: ここで大声で話すわけにはいかない。
examples.translation: I cannot speak loudly here.

commonMistakes: Using it as a plain synonym for できない.
Missing the change in meaning when the verb is negative.

grammar.title: すぎる
grammar.formation: Verb stem, い-adjective stem, or な-adjective stem + すぎる.
grammar.intuition: すぎる marks a degree that goes beyond what is appropriate or expected.
usageConditions: Remove い from an い-adjective before adding すぎる.
For verbs, use the ます-stem rather than the full ます-form.

examples.japanese: 昨日はお酒を飲みすぎました。
examples.translation: I drank too much alcohol yesterday.

examples.japanese: このかばんは重すぎます。
examples.translation: This bag is too heavy.

examples.japanese: この靴は小さすぎます。
examples.translation: These shoes are too small.

examples.japanese: 昨日は働きすぎました。
examples.translation: I worked too much yesterday.

commonMistakes: Keeping the full い-adjective ending before すぎる.
Using the dictionary form of a verb instead of its stem.

grammar.title: 中
grammar.formation: Noun or verb stem + 中（ちゅう）.
grammar.intuition: 中 marks the period during which an activity or situation is in progress.
usageConditions: Use it with an activity or period that is currently underway.
Reading and attachment depend on the word: for example, 会議中 and 勉強中.

examples.japanese: 今、会議中です。
examples.translation: I am in a meeting now.

examples.japanese: 旅行中に写真をたくさん撮りました。
examples.translation: I took many photos during the trip.

examples.japanese: 授業中は携帯電話を使いません。
examples.translation: I do not use my phone during class.

examples.japanese: 準備中なので、少し待ってください。
examples.translation: We are preparing, so please wait a little.

commonMistakes: Attaching 中 to an unsuitable completed event.
Ignoring the word-specific reading and usage.

grammar.title: 方
grammar.formation: Verb ます-stem + 方（かた）.
grammar.intuition: 方 turns an action into a named method or way of doing it.
usageConditions: Remove ます from the polite form before adding 方.
Use の when connecting the method noun to another noun where needed.

examples.japanese: この漢字の読み方を教えてください。
examples.translation: Please tell me how to read this kanji.

examples.japanese: 電車の乗り方が分かりません。
examples.translation: I do not know how to ride the train.

examples.japanese: このアプリの使い方を教えてください。
examples.translation: Please tell me how to use this app.

examples.japanese: 漢字の書き方を練習します。
examples.translation: I practice how to write kanji.

commonMistakes: Keeping ます before 方.
Confusing the method noun with a direct command to perform the verb.

grammar.title: と（conditional）
grammar.formation: Plain non-past form + と + result.
grammar.intuition: と links a condition to a predictable, automatic, or regularly repeated result.
usageConditions: Use it for natural laws, routines, instructions about what happens, or predictable results.
Do not normally use it when the result is a speaker's request, invitation, or intention.

examples.japanese: 春になると、桜が咲きます。
examples.translation: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

examples.japanese: このボタンを押すと、ドアが開きます。
examples.translation: When you press this button, the door opens.

examples.japanese: 冬になると、日が短くなります。
examples.translation: When winter comes, the days get shorter.

examples.japanese: この道をまっすぐ行くと、駅があります。
examples.translation: If you go straight on this road, there is a station.

commonMistakes: Do not use と for a one-time request or invitation in the result clause.
Keep the condition in the plain non-past form before と.

grammar.title: たら
grammar.formation: Verb, adjective, or noun past form + ら.
grammar.intuition: たら sets up a condition or completed point after which the next action or result is considered.
usageConditions: Use it for hypothetical conditions, future plans, requests, and a condition that has been reached.
Use the past form before ら even when the condition is about the future.

examples.japanese: 雨が降ったら、家にいます。
examples.translation: If it rains, I will stay home.

examples.japanese: 仕事が終わったら、連絡してください。
examples.translation: When you finish work, please contact me.

examples.japanese: 時間があったら、映画を見ます。
examples.translation: If I have time, I will watch a movie.

examples.japanese: 分からなかったら、先生に聞いてください。
examples.translation: If you do not understand, please ask the teacher.

commonMistakes: Do not replace the past form before ら with the dictionary form.
Choose たら when the result is a one-time plan, request, or decision rather than an automatic result.

grammar.title: ば
grammar.formation: Verb 仮定形: う段 changes to え段 + ば; ichidan verbs use れば; する becomes すれば; くる becomes くれば.
grammar.intuition: ば presents a condition as the requirement under which the result follows, often for advice or general reasoning.
usageConditions: Use it for conditions, recommendations, and results framed as a requirement.
For a natural negative condition, use the negative form + ければ.

examples.japanese: 安ければ、買います。
examples.translation: If it is cheap, I will buy it.

examples.japanese: この薬を飲めば、元気になります。
examples.translation: If you take this medicine, you will feel better.

examples.japanese: 分からなければ、もう一度説明します。
examples.translation: If you do not understand, I will explain it once more.

examples.japanese: 駅へ行けば、すぐ分かります。
examples.translation: If you go to the station, you will understand right away.

commonMistakes: Do not form ば by adding it directly to the dictionary form.
Remember that negative conditions use 〜なければ, not 〜ないば.

grammar.title: なら
grammar.meaning: if it is the case that; if you mean
grammar.formation: Noun or plain clause + なら; な-adjectives use the adjective stem + なら.
grammar.intuition: なら takes information already on the table and offers a response, judgment, or advice about that topic.
usageConditions: Use it when reacting to a stated or assumed topic or situation.
It is especially natural for recommendations and advice based on the listener's situation.

examples.japanese: 京都へ行くなら、秋がおすすめです。
examples.translation: If you are going to Kyoto, autumn is recommended.

examples.japanese: 時間があるなら、手伝ってください。
examples.translation: If you have time, please help me.

examples.japanese: 日本料理なら、この店が有名です。
examples.translation: If you mean Japanese food, this restaurant is famous.

examples.japanese: 明日なら、大丈夫です。
examples.translation: If it is tomorrow, that is fine.

commonMistakes: Do not treat なら as a neutral automatic-result conditional; it responds to a topic or premise.
Use なら after the plain clause or noun phrase that sets the topic.

grammar.title: 可能形（五段）
grammar.meaning: can do; be able to (godan verbs)
grammar.formation: Change the final う-sound of a godan verb to the matching え-sound and add る: 書く → 書ける, 読む → 読める.
grammar.intuition: The potential form turns an action into an ability or possibility available to the subject.
usageConditions: Use it for what the subject can or cannot do, including situational possibility.
The former object is commonly marked with が in potential sentences, especially in careful teaching examples.

examples.japanese: 私は日本語が少し話せます。
examples.translation: I can speak a little Japanese.

examples.japanese: この店ではカードが使えます。
examples.translation: You can use cards at this shop.

examples.japanese: この漢字が読めますか。
examples.translation: Can you read this kanji?

examples.japanese: 週末なら、一時間泳げます。
examples.translation: If it is the weekend, I can swim for an hour.

commonMistakes: Do not use the え-sound change for ichidan verbs such as 食べる; use 食べられる.
Do not confuse a potential form with a passive reading; use the surrounding subject and meaning to identify ability.

grammar.title: 可能形（一段）
grammar.meaning: can do; be able to (ichidan verbs)
grammar.formation: Remove る from an ichidan verb and add られる: 食べる → 食べられる, 見る → 見られる.
grammar.intuition: Ichidan potential forms describe an ability or possibility while sharing their shape with some passive and honorific forms.
usageConditions: Use the full られる form in the curriculum so it remains distinct from the passive form.
Interpret the form from its subject, object, and context rather than from the ending alone.

examples.japanese: 私は刺身が食べられます。
examples.translation: I can eat sashimi.

examples.japanese: ここから富士山が見られます。
examples.translation: You can see Mount Fuji from here.

examples.japanese: 一人で着替えられます。
examples.translation: I can change clothes by myself.

examples.japanese: 子どもはこの映画が見られません。
examples.translation: Children cannot watch this movie.

commonMistakes: Do not drop ら in formal potential practice: teach 食べられる and 見られる first.
Do not assume every られる form means potential; passive and honorific readings require different context.

grammar.title: ことができる
grammar.formation: Verb dictionary form + ことができる; negative ability uses ことができない.
grammar.intuition: ことができる states ability or permission in an explicit, neutral construction that works across verb classes.
usageConditions: Use it when a clear, explicit ability statement is more useful than a compact potential verb.
Keep the main verb in dictionary form before ことができる.

examples.japanese: 日本語でメールを書くことができます。
examples.translation: I can write emails in Japanese.

examples.japanese: この図書館で本を借りることができます。
examples.translation: You can borrow books at this library.

examples.japanese: オンラインで予約することができます。
examples.translation: You can make a reservation online.

examples.japanese: ここで写真を撮ることができません。
examples.translation: You cannot take photos here.

commonMistakes: Do not use the ます-form before ことができる; use the dictionary form.
Both potential verbs and ことができる express ability, but do not mix their formations in one sentence.

grammar.title: 受身形（五段）
grammar.meaning: be done to; be affected by (godan verbs)
grammar.formation: Change the final う-sound of a godan verb to the matching あ-sound and add れる: 書く → 書かれる, 読む → 読まれる.
grammar.intuition: The passive form puts the affected person or thing in focus instead of the agent's action.
usageConditions: Use に to mark the agent when naming who performed the action.
Use the passive when the subject is affected by an event; this is different from saying what the subject can do.

examples.japanese: 私は先生に名前を呼ばれました。
examples.translation: My name was called by the teacher.

examples.japanese: 弟は母にしかられました。
examples.translation: My younger brother was scolded by our mother.

examples.japanese: この歌は多くの人に歌われています。
examples.translation: This song is sung by many people.

examples.japanese: 電車の中で足を踏まれました。
examples.translation: Someone stepped on my foot on the train.

commonMistakes: Do not form godan passive with the え-sound used by potential: 書く becomes 書かれる, not 書けられる.
Use に for the agent and は or が for the affected subject when the roles need to be clear.

grammar.title: 受身形（一段）
grammar.meaning: be done to; be affected by (ichidan verbs)
grammar.formation: Remove る from an ichidan verb and add られる: 食べる → 食べられる, 見る → 見られる.
grammar.intuition: Ichidan passive forms share their shape with potential forms, so the subject's role and the presence of an agent determine the meaning.
usageConditions: Use に for the person or thing that performs the action when it matters.
Check whether the subject is affected or able: passive and potential readings cannot be separated by the ending alone.

examples.japanese: 私は友達に笑われました。
examples.translation: I was laughed at by my friend.

examples.japanese: その本は多くの人に読まれています。
examples.translation: That book is read by many people.

examples.japanese: 子どもは先生にほめられました。
examples.translation: The child was praised by the teacher.

examples.japanese: 私は弟にケーキを食べられました。
examples.translation: My younger brother ate my cake, to my annoyance.

commonMistakes: Do not interpret every られる form as ability; an explicit agent with に often signals passive meaning.
Keep the affected subject as the sentence topic instead of treating the agent as the subject.

grammar.title: 使役形（五段）
grammar.meaning: make or let someone do (godan verbs)
grammar.formation: Change the final う-sound of a godan verb to the matching あ-sound and add せる: 読む → 読ませる, 書く → 書かせる.
grammar.intuition: The causative form makes the subject responsible for causing or allowing another person to act.
usageConditions: Mark the person caused to act with に for many transitive actions and with を for many intransitive actions.
Use context to distinguish making someone act from giving them permission to act.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に本を読ませました。
examples.translation: The teacher made the students read a book.

examples.japanese: 母は子どもに野菜を食べさせました。
examples.translation: The mother made her child eat vegetables.

examples.japanese: 部長は私を駅まで行かせました。
examples.translation: The manager made me go to the station.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生を早く帰らせました。
examples.translation: The teacher let the students go home early.

commonMistakes: Do not use the え-sound used by godan potential; 読む becomes 読ませる, not 読めさせる.
Choose に or を according to the action's argument structure and keep the causer as the grammatical subject.

grammar.title: 使役形（一段）
grammar.meaning: make or let someone do (ichidan verbs)
grammar.formation: Remove る from an ichidan verb and add させる: 食べる → 食べさせる, 見る → 見させる.
grammar.intuition: The ichidan causative form keeps the causer in control while showing the other person's action or permission.
usageConditions: Name the causee when it matters and use the polite or plain ending required by the sentence.
Do not confuse させる with passive or potential られる forms.

examples.japanese: 母は子どもに野菜を食べさせました。
examples.translation: The mother made her child eat vegetables.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に映画を見させました。
examples.translation: The teacher made the students watch a movie.

examples.japanese: 父は私を早く起きさせました。
examples.translation: My father made me get up early.

examples.japanese: 母は赤ちゃんを寝させました。
examples.translation: The mother put the baby to sleep.

commonMistakes: Do not attach させる directly to the dictionary form of an ichidan verb; 食べる becomes 食べさせる.
Keep the person who makes or allows the action as the subject, not the person who performs the embedded action.

grammar.title: 意向形
grammar.formation: Godan verbs change the final う-sound to the お-sound and add う: 読む → 読もう. Ichidan verbs drop る and add よう: 食べる → 食べよう.
grammar.intuition: The volitional form presents a proposal or the speaker's intention to act.
usageConditions: Use it alone for an informal proposal or with と思います／と思っています for a stated intention.
Use the polite proposal ましょう when the situation calls for a more formal or direct invitation.

examples.japanese: 週末に映画を見ようと思います。
examples.translation: I intend to watch a movie this weekend.

examples.japanese: 明日から毎日歩こうと思っています。
examples.translation: I am planning to walk every day starting tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べよう。
examples.translation: Let's eat lunch together.

examples.japanese: 次の電車に乗ろうと思います。
examples.translation: I think I will take the next train.

commonMistakes: Do not use the godan お-sound change for ichidan verbs: 食べる becomes 食べよう, not 食べおう.
Distinguish an immediate proposal よう from an intention softened or framed by と思います／と思っています.

grammar.title: あげる・くれる・もらう
grammar.meaning: give; receive; someone gives to me or my side
grammar.formation: Use あげる when the subject gives, くれる when someone gives to the speaker's side, and もらう when the subject receives; mark the giver or receiver with に／が as the perspective requires.
grammar.intuition: The three verbs describe one transfer from different viewpoints: outward from the giver, toward the speaker's side, or from the receiver's viewpoint.
usageConditions: Use くれる for a gift coming to the speaker or someone in the speaker's group, not for a neutral third-party transfer.
Choose the verb from the sentence subject's perspective before choosing the particle for the other person.

examples.japanese: 私は友達にプレゼントをあげました。
examples.translation: I gave my friend a present.

examples.japanese: 友達が私に本をくれました。
examples.translation: My friend gave me a book.

examples.japanese: 私は先生に辞書をもらいました。
examples.translation: I received a dictionary from my teacher.

examples.japanese: 姉に花をあげました。
examples.translation: I gave flowers to my older sister.

commonMistakes: Do not use くれる when the gift does not come to the speaker's side; use あげる for an outward transfer.
Do not confuse the giver perspective of くれる with the receiver perspective of もらう.

grammar.title: てある
grammar.meaning: has been done and remains that way
grammar.formation: Transitive verb て-form + ある; the resulting state is described with the affected object as the topic or subject.
grammar.intuition: てある highlights a deliberate action whose result has been left in place for a purpose.
usageConditions: Use a transitive verb when someone intentionally creates the state.
Contrast it with ている when the focus is the resulting arrangement rather than the action or a natural state.

examples.japanese: 机の上に資料が置いてあります。
examples.translation: The materials have been placed on the desk.

examples.japanese: 会議室のドアが開けてあります。
examples.translation: The meeting-room door has been left open.

examples.japanese: 旅行の準備がしてあります。
examples.translation: The preparations for the trip have been made.

examples.japanese: 壁に予定が書いてあります。
examples.translation: The schedule has been written on the wall.

commonMistakes: Do not use an intransitive verb for the deliberate arrangement pattern; choose the transitive action that created the state.
Do not reduce てある to simple present location; it carries a remaining result and an intentional setup.

grammar.title: ていた
grammar.meaning: was doing; used to be; had been
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + いた; polite speech uses ていました.
grammar.intuition: ていた places an ongoing action, repeated habit, or state inside a past time frame.
usageConditions: Use it for an action in progress at a past reference point or a past state that no longer holds.
Use surrounding time words and context to distinguish one ongoing event from a former habit.

examples.japanese: 昨日の午後、図書館で勉強していました。
examples.translation: I was studying at the library yesterday afternoon.

examples.japanese: 子どものころ、よく川で遊んでいました。
examples.translation: When I was a child, I often played by the river.

examples.japanese: 以前、この町に住んでいました。
examples.translation: I used to live in this town.

examples.japanese: 電話したとき、彼は寝ていました。
examples.translation: When I called, he was sleeping.

commonMistakes: Do not use ていた for a completed single event when the ongoing or former-state meaning is not intended.
Keep the past auxiliary いた／いました after the て-form; do not stop at ている for a past-time context.

grammarContrasts.title: ていく and てくる
grammarContrasts.explanation: ていく points an action or change away from the present and forward. てくる brings an action back toward the speaker or marks a change that has begun to appear.

examples.japanese: これからも勉強していきます。
examples.translation: I will keep studying from now on.

examples.japanese: 最近、少し分かってきました。
examples.translation: Recently, I have started to understand a little.

exercises: Choose ていく for a change continuing away from now.
Choose てくる for a change that has begun to reach the present.

grammarContrasts.title: てあげる・てくれる・てもらう
grammarContrasts.explanation: The three forms describe the same kind of help from different viewpoints: offering a favor, receiving someone else's favor, or receiving the favor as the grammatical focus.

examples.japanese: 友達に本を貸してあげました。
examples.translation: I lent a book to my friend as a favor.

examples.japanese: 先生に作文を見てもらいました。
examples.translation: I had the teacher look over my composition.

exercises: Use てあげる when the subject offers the action to someone else.
Use てくれる or てもらう when the speaker's side receives the benefit.

grammarContrasts.title: Strong inference and appearance
grammarContrasts.explanation: に違いない and に決まっている make strong judgments. みたい and らしい can sound less definite and depend more on resemblance, appearance, hearsay, or typicality in context.

examples.japanese: 彼は疲れているに違いない。
examples.translation: He must be tired.

examples.japanese: 雨が降るみたいです。
examples.translation: It seems like it will rain.

exercises: Choose a strong-certainty form when the speaker makes an emphatic conclusion.
Choose みたい or らしい when the context signals appearance, hearsay, or typicality.

grammarContrasts.title: と・たら・ば・なら
grammarContrasts.explanation: と favors predictable or automatic results, たら handles hypothetical or completed conditions with plans and requests, ば frames a requirement or recommendation, and なら responds to an already stated topic or premise.

examples.japanese: 春になると、桜が咲きます。
examples.translation: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

examples.japanese: 京都へ行くなら、秋がおすすめです。
examples.translation: If you are going to Kyoto, autumn is recommended.

exercises: Choose と for a predictable or automatic result.
Choose たら, ば, or なら when the context calls for a plan, requirement, or topic-based recommendation.

grammarContrasts.title: Potential verbs and ことができる
grammarContrasts.explanation: Godan verbs change to the え-sound, ichidan verbs use られる, and ことができる keeps the main verb in dictionary form. The potential verb is compact; ことができる is more explicit and works uniformly across verb classes.

examples.japanese: 漢字が読めます。
examples.translation: I can read kanji.

examples.japanese: 漢字を読むことができます。
examples.translation: I can read kanji.

exercises: Choose the godan or ichidan potential formation based on the verb class.
Choose ことができる when an explicit, uniform ability construction is the better fit.

grammarContrasts.title: Passive and potential られる
grammarContrasts.explanation: Godan passive uses the あ-sound plus れる while godan potential uses the え-sound plus る. Ichidan passive and potential share られる, so the subject's role, agent marker, and sentence meaning determine which reading is intended.

examples.japanese: 先生に名前を呼ばれました。
examples.translation: My name was called by the teacher.

examples.japanese: 日本語が話せます。
examples.translation: I can speak Japanese.

exercises: Choose passive when the subject is affected by an agent marked with に.
Choose potential when the subject's ability or possibility is the focus.

grammarContrasts.title: Causative godan and ichidan forms
grammarContrasts.explanation: Godan verbs change to the あ-sound plus せる, while ichidan verbs drop る and take させる. Both forms make or allow another person to act, with the causee marked according to the embedded verb's argument structure.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に本を読ませました。
examples.translation: The teacher made the students read a book.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に映画を見させました。
examples.translation: The teacher made the students watch a movie.

exercises: Choose the causative ending from the verb class before deciding whether the meaning is make or let.
Identify the causer, causee, and embedded action before choosing に or を.
